prompt: In the stack trace of a panic, which frame comes first, right under the `goroutine` line?
hint: In `~/stacks` it was `main.unitPrice`.

choices.text: `main.main`, because the program starts there
choices.why: `main.main` came last. The trace is printed from the other end.

choices.text: The function that was running when the panic happened
choices.why: Right. Frames are printed deepest first, so the top one is where the program broke.

choices.text: The function that was called first by the program, after the runtime had started it and handed it control
choices.why: That is the order the calls were made in, which the figure drew on the left; the trace prints the right-hand order.

choices.text: The runtime's own panic function
choices.why: The default trace leaves the runtime's frames out; `~/stacks` showed only `main` functions.

prompt: The trace of `~/stacks` has `main.lineTotal(...)` above `/home/ana/stacks/main.go:21`. What is on line 21?
hint: Every frame but the top one points at a call.

choices.text: The index that went out of range
choices.why: That is line 17, the top frame's line, `discount[qty]`.

choices.text: The declaration `func lineTotal(l line) int`
choices.why: A frame's line is where the function was when the trace was taken, not where the function begins.

choices.text: The call from `lineTotal` to `unitPrice`
choices.why: Right. Below the top frame, each frame's line is where that function made the call above it.

choices.text: The call from `orderTotal` to `lineTotal`
choices.why: That call is line 27, in the `orderTotal` frame below.

prompt: `main.main` calls `run`, `run` calls `load`, and `load` calls `parseLine`, which panics. Put the frames in the order the trace prints them.
hint: Deepest first.

prompt: Three frames of the `~/stacks` trace end in `(...)` and have no `+0x` after their line. Why?
hint: `go build -gcflags=-m` answered it.

choices.text: Those functions took no arguments
choices.why: `unitPrice` takes two, and with inlining off the runtime printed them.

choices.text: The runtime hid the arguments because they held private data
choices.why: The runtime does not judge the data; with `-l` it printed `{0x49b0c7?, 0x41b4f9?}, 0x4` for the same call.

choices.text: The compiler inlined them, copying their bodies into the caller
choices.why: Right. There was no separate call at run time, so there are no arguments and no offset to print.

choices.text: The trace was cut short because it was too long
choices.why: Nothing was cut: the file and line of each frame are all there, down to `main.main`.

prompt: A crash ends at `main.go:34 +0x15b`. A colleague edits a different function, rebuilds, gets the same crash, and sees `main.go:34 +0x163`. Is it a different bug?
hint: What is the offset measured from, and in which binary?

choices.text: Yes: a different offset means a different instruction failed
choices.why: Different instruction in a different binary; the offset is only comparable within one build.

choices.text: Yes, because the edit moved the bug to another place in `main`
choices.why: The line is still 34, and the line is what keeps its meaning across builds.

choices.text: It cannot be known without a debugger
choices.why: The trace already answers it: same function, same file, same line.

choices.text: Almost certainly not: same line; the offset moves whenever the machine code is rebuilt
choices.why: Right. `+0x` is the distance from the function's start in this binary, so read the line instead.

prompt: What did `GOTRACEBACK=none ./stacks` print?
hint: It is the setting that takes something away.

choices.text: Nothing, and the exit status was 0
choices.why: The message stayed and the status was still 2; the setting changes what is printed, not how the program ends.

choices.text: The `panic:` line and no frames
choices.why: Right. The message and the exit status survive and every frame is gone.

choices.text: The traces of the runtime's goroutines as well as the program's
choices.why: That is `system`, the opposite end of the scale.

choices.text: The default trace, because `none` is not a valid value
choices.why: `none` is in the documentation and it worked: the frames were missing.

prompt: A server panics in a goroutine that was waiting on another goroutine it had started. Which `GOTRACEBACK` shows both?
hint: The documentation's word for goroutines the program created.

choices.text: `single`, the default
choices.why: The default prints the current goroutine only.

choices.text: `all`
choices.why: Right. It adds the traces of every user-created goroutine.

choices.text: `none`, and a `debug.Stack` call in each goroutine instead
choices.why: `debug.Stack` shows only the goroutine that calls it, and `none` removes the frames you wanted.

choices.text: `crash`, which adds the other goroutines to the trace
choices.why: `all` and `system` already do; `crash` adds a core dump on top of `system`.

prompt: `debug.Stack()` was called inside `price`'s deferred function, after the panic. Why did its trace still show `main.unitPrice` and line 22?
hint: Where does a deferred function run while a panic is under way?

choices.text: `debug.Stack` returns the trace of the last panic, saved by the runtime
choices.why: Its documentation says it formats the trace of the goroutine that calls it, as it is now.

choices.text: `slog.Error` added the frames when it logged the value that `recover` had returned to the deferred function
choices.why: The `slog` line was one line of key=value pairs; the frames came from `debug.Stack`.

choices.text: The deferred function runs on top of the frames that panicked, before they are removed
choices.why: Right. That is why a trace taken there still reaches the line of the bug.

choices.text: `recover` puts the panicking frames back on the stack
choices.why: Nothing is put back: the frames were never gone, and `debug.Stack` ran before `price` returned.

prompt: `slog.Error("order failed", "order", id, ...)` printed `order=2`: after the message, `slog` takes its arguments in pairs and writes each pair as ___=value.
hint: The first of each pair is what a log system searches by.

prompt: A service recovers each request's panic and logs only `panic="runtime error: index out of range [4] with length 4"`. What does the person on call lack, and how is it fixed?
hint: Which part of the output is about where?

choices.text: Nothing: the message names the index and the length, which is enough to find the line
choices.why: Any slice indexed anywhere could have printed it; the message has no file and no line.

choices.text: The frames: log `debug.Stack()` with the line, from the deferred function
choices.why: Right. The runtime prints no trace for a recovered panic, so the program has to write it.

choices.text: The frames: set `GOTRACEBACK=all` so the runtime prints them
choices.why: `GOTRACEBACK` only shapes the trace of a panic that kills the program; this one was recovered.

choices.text: The exit status, which says which handler panicked
choices.why: A recovered panic does not end the process, and a status names no handler anyway.

prompt: Which command shows the commit a Go binary was built from, without running the binary?
hint: It read `vcs.revision` out of `stacks`.

choices.text: `git log --oneline`
choices.why: That lists the repository's commits; it cannot say which one a given binary came from.

choices.text: `go version -m`
choices.why: Right. It prints the module, the Go release and the build settings, `vcs.revision` included.

choices.text: `go doc runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo`
choices.why: That prints the documentation of the function a program calls to read its own record.

choices.text: `file`, which prints the BuildID
choices.why: The BuildID identifies the build's content, not the commit; `vcs.revision` is the commit.

prompt: A binary's record says `vcs.modified=true`. What does that tell you during an incident?
hint: Read the `BuildSetting` documentation again.

choices.text: The binary file was changed on disk at some point after the go command had built it
choices.why: The setting describes the source tree at build time, not the file afterwards.

choices.text: The module has a newer version available
choices.why: Nothing in the record looks at other versions; it describes this build.

choices.text: Go was upgraded since the commit
choices.why: The Go release has its own line, `go1.27.1`; `vcs.modified` is about the tree.

choices.text: The tree had uncommitted changes, so the commit alone does not describe the code
choices.why: Right. With `false` the revision is the exact source; with `true` some of the code exists only on the machine that built it.

prompt: `go build -ldflags=-s` produced `small`. Which of these did the binary lose? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare `./small`'s trace and `go version -m small` with the full build.

choices.text: The symbol table
choices.why: Yes: the linker's help says `-s` omits it.

choices.text: The DWARF debug information
choices.why: Yes: `-s` implies `-w`, which omits the DWARF symbol table.

choices.text: The file and line in its traces
choices.why: No: `./small` still printed `main.go:20`.

choices.text: The module version and commit `go version -m` reads
choices.why: No: `go version -m small` still showed `v0.0.0-20261006130000-d569db795b44`.

prompt: Built with `-trimpath`, what did the last frame of the trace say instead of `/home/ana/stacks-release/main.go:53`?
hint: The recorded file names begin with something the module declares.

choices.text: `main.go:53`, with no directory at all
choices.why: Something replaces the directory; the trace showed what.

choices.text: `./main.go:53`, relative to where the build ran
choices.why: That would still depend on the builder's directory, which is what `-trimpath` removes.

choices.text: `example.com/stacks/main.go:53`
choices.why: Right. The module path took the place of the home directory, and the line stayed 53.

choices.text: Nothing: `-trimpath` removes the file names from traces
choices.why: It removes file system paths, not file names; the frame still named `main.go`.

prompt: `stacks` was 2430545 bytes and the stripped `small` 1568928. By how many percent, rounded to a whole number, did stripping shrink the binary?
hint: Divide the difference by the larger size.

prompt: Match each piece of a trace with what it means.
hint: Section 02 read each one.

pairs.right: Which goroutine the frames below belong to, and its state
A function the compiler inlined into its caller
Where the instruction sits in the function's machine code
An argument value the runtime cannot vouch for

right_distractors: The number of times the function was called

prompt: A trace's top frame is `regexp.MustCompile` in `/usr/local/go/src/regexp/regexp.go:312`, and the next is `main.init()` at `main.go:11`. Where do you start looking for the bug?
hint: Lesson 36 printed this trace.

choices.text: At `regexp.go:312`, since the top frame is where the program broke
choices.why: It broke there on purpose: `MustCompile` panics when it is given a bad pattern. The mistake is the pattern it was given.

choices.text: At `main.go:11`, the first frame in your own code
choices.why: Right. Read down past the library's frames to the first call your code made; there the bad pattern was passed in.

choices.text: In `main.main`, where the trace ends
choices.why: This one has no `main.main` frame: the panic came before `main` ran.

choices.text: In the Go release, since a standard library function panicked
choices.why: `MustCompile` did what its documentation says it does with a pattern that does not parse.

prompt: `main.unitPrice({0x49b0c7?, 0x41b4f9?}, 0x4)`. Which printed value can you trust?
hint: Look for the one without a mark.

choices.text: `0x41b4f9`, the length of the string
choices.why: It carries a `?`, and no string `"cake"` is four million bytes long.

choices.text: All three, since the runtime read them from the stack
choices.why: The `?` marks the ones it could not vouch for: the slot was no longer in use.

choices.text: None: arguments in a trace are always stale
choices.why: The unmarked one matched the message exactly, index 4.

choices.text: `0x4`, the quantity
choices.why: Right. It has no `?`, and it is the 4 the panic message named.

prompt: A crash in production points at `main.go:20`, and line 20 of `main.go` on your machine today is a blank line. What do you do first?
hint: The binary knows something your checkout does not.

choices.text: Conclude the trace is wrong because the binary was stripped
choices.why: A stripped binary printed the right file and line in section 04.

choices.text: Rebuild from your checkout and wait for the crash to happen again
choices.why: Your checkout is not the code that crashed; the new binary's lines may not match either.

choices.text: Read `vcs.revision` from the binary and look at line 20 of `main.go` in that commit
choices.why: Right. `go version -m` or the logged version gives the commit, and `git show <rev>:main.go` gives the line.

choices.text: Search the code for the panic message instead of using the line
choices.why: A runtime message such as `index out of range` is not in your code; the line is the precise part.

prompt: Inside a deferred function, `debug.___()` returns the trace of the goroutine that calls it, as bytes a logger can write.
hint: A function of `runtime/debug`.
